summary: Describes authenticating IS-IS protocol data units using the HMAC-MD5 algorithm, in addition to the plain-text password mechanism in the base specification. This gives routers a way to check that routing messages come from trusted neighbors and were not altered. It replaced RFC 3567 and was later updated.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5304 adds HMAC-MD5 authentication to IS-IS routing messages. A router uses a shared password to calculate a check value, and a receiving router rejects a message when its value does not match. The RFC replaces RFC 3567 and has been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

questions: how to secure is-is routing messages
subtitle: How IS-IS routers use a keyed message check to reject altered routing messages.

tldr.problem: The base IS-IS specification defines authentication with a cleartext password, but allows for multiple authentication algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5304 assigns authentication type 54 to HMAC-MD5. A router computes the value over the PDU with selected fields set to zero, using the password for that PDU type as the key.
tldr.outcome: Routers that support HMAC-MD5 must discard messages with an incorrect value. This RFC replaces RFC 3567 and is updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

today: RFC 5304 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 3567, updates RFC 1195, and has been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

sections.title: Authentication for IS-IS Messages
sections.content:
IS-IS routers exchange Link State Protocol Data Units (LSPs), which carry information used by the routing protocol. The base IS-IS specification includes an authentication field, but specifies only a cleartext-password algorithm.

This RFC adds HMAC-MD5 as another way to authenticate protocol data units (PDUs). It also describes changes needed to make that authentication work. RFC 5304 replaces RFC 3567 and updates RFC 1195.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS routers share routing information in messages called PDUs. This RFC lets them use HMAC-MD5 to check those messages, alongside the original password method.

sections.title: The Authentication Information Field
sections.content:
Authentication information is carried in a Type-Length-Value (TLV) field. Its type is 10. The first octet of its value identifies the authentication method; any remaining octets hold that method's Authentication Value.

RFC 5304 assigns type 54 (0x36) to HMAC-MD5. Its Authentication Value is 16 octets long, making the TLV length field 17. Other values already include reserved type 0, cleartext-password type 1 and routing-domain-private type 255.
sections.plainLanguage: The authentication TLV has a number that identifies its method, followed by the method's value. Type 54 identifies HMAC-MD5, whose check value occupies 16 octets.

sections.title: Calculating and Verifying HMAC-MD5
sections.content:
The key is the password for the PDU type, as specified by ISO 10589. The input is the whole PDU with the Authentication Value set to zero; the type and TLV length are set before calculation. For an LSP, the Checksum and Remaining Lifetime fields are also zero during calculation. The result is placed in the Authentication Value.

Different PDU types use their corresponding authentication string: Level 1 and Level 2 Sequence Number PDUs use the area and domain strings, and Hello PDUs use the link-level string. A router verifies a received value by saving it and the relevant checksum and lifetime fields, zeroing them, calculating again, and restoring them. An implementation of HMAC-MD5 MUST discard a PDU with an incorrect value.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates a check value over the message with specified fields blanked out. The receiver repeats that calculation with the shared password. If the values differ, an implementation that supports HMAC-MD5 must discard the message.

sections.title: Transition and LSP Purge Rules
sections.content:
During a gradual rollout, an implementation MAY add HMAC-MD5 information without checking it. It MAY also test several passwords, which allows a network to change passwords incrementally. An implementation without HMAC-MD5 support MAY accept a PDU carrying this authentication type.

A router that supports HMAC-MD5 and initiates an LSP purge MUST remove the LSP body and add the authentication TLV. It MUST reject unauthenticated purges and purges containing other TLVs. These rules prevent a system without the password from setting an LSP's Remaining Lifetime to zero and flooding it as a purge.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can add authentication before they begin checking it, which supports a gradual changeover. A purge from a router using HMAC-MD5 must carry authentication and no other TLVs, so an outsider cannot start one without the password.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers After a Password Change
sections.content:
A router may restart just after changing its password. Its LSP Sequence Number can then restart at 1 under the new password, while neighbors still hold a higher number. They reject the new LSPs as older, and the router cannot authenticate old versions that neighbors send back.

One suggested solution is for the process to notice an incoming LSP with its own System ID, a higher sequence number and a failed authentication check. It SHOULD raise its sequence number and flood the LSPs again. Because an attacker could trigger this condition, the RFC recommends keeping a counter for it.
sections.plainLanguage: After a restart during a password change, a router may send low sequence numbers that neighbors reject. The RFC suggests noticing higher-numbered messages for the router's own ID and raising its number, while counting these events because an attacker could cause them.

sections.title: Security Limits and Key Handling
sections.content:
The goal is to make it harder for an attacker to inject false routing information; keeping routing information secret is not a goal. The mechanism does not prevent replay attacks, though existing IS-IS mechanisms would reject old information in most cases. It also does not protect against denial of service or compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured routers.

Security depends on the algorithm, a strong and confidential key, and correct implementations on all communicating routers. The RFC discusses published attacks on MD5 and states that, at the time of writing, none applied to HMAC-MD5 as used here; it notes that future attacks remain possible. It strongly recommends support for keys made of printable ASCII strings of 80 bytes or less.
sections.plainLanguage: HMAC-MD5 makes it harder to inject false routing information, but it does not stop replay attacks or protect against a compromised router. Its protection depends on correct software and keeping the shared password secret. The RFC also notes that future cryptographic attacks may be found.

sections.title: Authentication Type Registry
sections.content: The RFC establishes the IANA registry named IS-IS Authentication Type Codes for TLV 10. Values are recorded in decimal, and future assignments use Expert Review. The intended practice is to accompany allocations with a published specification, though an expert may approve an allocation when publication of an RFC is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: An IANA registry records which authentication method each TLV type number identifies. Expert Review governs future assignments.
